cues.text: Let us now turn to national and international frameworks, the legal structures that actually govern intellectual property, first inside Nigeria, and then across borders.
Begin with Nigeria.
Nigeria's Copyright Act 2022 provides modern protection for copyright works, and this includes computer programs.
So if you write software, the Copyright Act 2022 is the starting point for protecting that work as a copyright work.
The body that administers and enforces copyright within its mandate is the Nigerian Copyright Commission, which you will often see abbreviated as the NCC.
Notice the qualification here: the NCC acts within its mandate.
It is not an all-powerful authority over every intellectual property question.
Copyright is only one system.
The Patent and Designs Act and the Trade Marks Act provide distinct protection systems.
Distinct is the key word.
Patents and designs are handled under one law, trademarks under another, and each is separate from copyright.
These systems are administered through the relevant national registries, and when disputes arise, courts determine them.
So the registry grants and records the right, and the court resolves the conflict.
Now an important point about territory.
Nigeria's law and procedures govern local rights.
Foreign registration does not automatically grant local patents or trademarks.
Imagine a company that holds a patent or a trademark registered abroad.
That registration does not, by itself, give it a Nigerian patent or a Nigerian trademark.
Rights in Nigeria depend on Nigerian law and Nigerian procedures.
Next, the international institutions and treaties.
I will take them one at a time.
First, WIPO, the World Intellectual Property Organization.
WIPO facilitates international intellectual property cooperation, treaties and registration systems.
Be careful with one common misunderstanding: it is not a single world court.
WIPO helps countries cooperate and provides systems, but it does not sit as one global judge over every dispute.
Second, the Berne Convention.
It establishes automatic copyright protection without formalities, and it provides national treatment in member states, always subject to treaty scope.
Automatic means an author does not need to register in order to gain protection.
National treatment means that a member state gives works from other member states the same protection it gives its own nationals' works.
And remember the qualification: this operates within the scope of the treaty.
Third, TRIPS, which is the agreement associated with the World Trade Organization, the WTO.
TRIPS sets minimum intellectual property standards and enforcement obligations for its members.
Think of the word minimum: it sets a floor, a baseline that members must meet, along with obligations about enforcement.
Fourth, the Paris Convention.
It addresses industrial property, and it deals with priority and national treatment.
Industrial property is the area that covers things like patents and trademarks, as distinct from copyright.
Fifth, the Patent Cooperation Treaty, known as the PCT.
It facilitates international patent applications.
But note carefully: it does not itself grant a worldwide patent.
There is no such thing as a single patent that the PCT hands out for the whole world.
It makes the application process across countries easier.
Sixth, the Madrid System.
It facilitates international trademark registration among participating jurisdictions.
Yet territorial examination and protection still matter.
In other words, even with this system, each participating territory still has its own examination, and protection remains tied to territory.
Seventh, the WIPO Copyright Treaty.
It addresses copyright in the digital environment, which is directly relevant to software and online content.
Eighth, regional organisations, such as ARIPO and OAPI.
They support regional mechanisms for participating states.
The source gives a practical instruction here: check membership and national legal effect.
That means you must verify whether a given state participates, and what legal effect the regional mechanism actually has within that nation.
Finally, let us pull these ideas together under national sovereignty.
National sovereignty permits differing implementation, patent eligibility, exceptions, procedure, remedies and evidence rules.
So even when countries share treaties, they may implement them differently.
What can be patented, what exceptions apply, what procedures are followed, what remedies a court can award, and what rules govern evidence can all vary from one country to another.
This makes cross-border enforcement complicated.
It involves jurisdiction, forum, applicable law, the location of evidence, contracts, recognition of judgments and costs.
Ask yourself: which country's court has the power to hear the case, which forum is chosen, which country's law applies, where the evidence physically sits, what the parties agreed in their contracts,
whether a judgment from one country will be recognised in another, and how much all of this will cost.
Consider cloud hosting in another country.
It complicates investigation, because evidence and systems may sit abroad.
But it does not automatically eliminate rights.
The rights holder does not lose protection simply because the infrastructure is located elsewhere.
So the practical guidance is this: for real disputes, use clear contracts, keep good records, and obtain local legal advice.
This is educational material, not individual legal advice, and a real dispute needs a qualified lawyer in the relevant jurisdiction.
